aspects.title: A genuine content section in a multi-section page has no heading while sibling sections are headed
aspects.description: The heart of 2.4.10 is providing a heading for EACH section when a page is organized into sections, not merely 'the document has a heading somewhere.' The realistic violation is a page divided into several topical content sections where most carry headings but one substantive, topically-distinct section is left un-headed (e.g. a headed 'Abstract', 'Introduction', 'Results', 'Discussion' with a 500-word 'Methods' block of new subject matter wedged between two headed sections carrying only a bold first sentence and no heading). Recognizing that the un-headed prose is a distinct section that 'introduces' new subject matter — and therefore needs its own heading — requires reading the body and topically segmenting it, which is semantic human judgment.
aspects.scLimb: CORE: 'headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections... When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them' — the per-section obligation, not the binary document-has-a-heading proxy.
aspects.whyUncovered: Every ACT failure (7505d/81d501/929079/4e34ca) removes or hides the ONE heading of the ONE non-repeated #main block, so the corpus encodes only the binary 'document has a heading at all.' There is NO case with 3+ sibling content sections where one mid-document section is missing its heading while others are headed, so the actual 'heading for EACH section' obligation is untested. Automated checkers (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse) cannot detect this: the page contains valid headings and valid HTML; deciding that a particular un-headed prose block is a separate section needing its own heading requires reading and topically segmenting the content.

references.quote: The intent of this success criterion is to provide headings for sections of a web page, when the page is organized into sections. For instance, long documents are often divided into a variety of chapters, chapters have subtopics, etc. When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them.
Check that the content is divided into separate sections. Check that each section on the page starts with a heading.
Examine a page with content organized into sections. Check that a heading for each section exists.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build a single self-contained HTML page that is clearly organized into multiple topical sections, with real (not Lorem) prose so the topic shifts are perceptible. Give all-but-one section a programmatic heading (h2/h3) and leave exactly one substantive, topically-distinct section with NO heading (only a bold lead sentence or a plain paragraph). The page must still PASS axe-core / 047fe0 (it has page-level headings), so the failure is purely the missing per-section heading. Vary which position the un-headed section occupies (first, middle, last) so the gap is not always trailing.
suggestedScenarios: Research article with h2 'Abstract', h2 'Introduction', then a clearly-distinct 500-word 'Methods' discussion with NO heading, followed by h2 'Results' and h2 'Discussion' — the un-headed Methods block is a section missing its heading.
Product page with headed sections 'Overview', 'Specifications', 'Reviews', but a substantial 'Warranty & Returns' block of text wedged between Specifications and Reviews carrying no heading.
Recipe page with h2 'Ingredients' and h2 'Instructions' headed, but a long 'Tips & Variations' section (clearly a new topic) appended with only a bold first sentence and no heading.
How-to article whose first three steps are under h3 headings, then a fourth equally-substantial step block appears as a bare paragraph (its heading deleted), then h3 step five resumes.
FAQ page where most question groups carry h2 group headings ('Billing', 'Shipping') but one equally large group ('Account Security') is presented as a bare list with no preceding heading.

Restaurant menu (the Understanding example) where 'Appetizers', 'Soup', 'Entree', 'Dessert' carry h2 headings but the 'Salad' course sits between them with only larger bold text and no heading element.

aspects.title: Visually-demarcated sections (cards, columns, bands, rules, big gaps) with no programmatic heading for each
aspects.description: The Understanding explicitly warns that 'visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections,' yet a very common pattern lays a page out as visually obvious sections — boxed cards, color-banded rows, multi-column blocks, large whitespace gaps, horizontal rules, or tab panels — where each visual block is plainly a distinct section to a sighted user but NONE carries a programmatic heading. The page may have a single page-level h1 (so 047fe0's non-repeated-block check passes) while the several visually-demarcated content sections beneath it use only styled bold leading text, a CSS border, or color to signal a new section. A human must perceive that the layout communicates multiple sections to sighted users and confirm those sections lack the headings that would convey the same structure to AT users.
aspects.scLimb: 'Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections' — applied across MULTIPLE visually-implied sections, not the single-block template.
aspects.whyUncovered: ACT exercises the 'visual not sufficient' limb only inside the single-heading template: 7505d (one big bold strong = visual-only, FAIL) and 33fcbd (one <hr> alongside one real heading, PASS). It never builds a multi-section page where visual layout alone (cards/columns/bands/gaps/tabs) implies several sections without a programmatic heading for each. Automated tools cannot infer from CSS layout, whitespace, borders, or background color that a sighted user perceives several headed-looking sections — perceiving a visual section boundary and judging that it lacks a programmatic heading is inherently a visual + semantic human judgment.

references.quote: Other page elements may complement headings to improve presentation (e.g., horizontal rules and boxes), but visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections.
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
Examine a page with content organized into sections. Check that a heading for each section exists.

(or styled ), not a heading element and not role=heading. Keep a single page-level h1 so axe/047fe0 pass. The required verdict is FAIL because each perceived section lacks a programmatic heading. Render and screenshot to confirm the visual section boundaries are unmistakable to a sighted viewer.

Marketing landing page of full-width color-banded stripes (each a different topic) where every band's title is a styled

rather than a heading, under one page h1.
Two-column article where left column 'Features' and right column 'Pricing' are visually separate sections but both leads are <span class='title'> with no heading markup.

Tabbed settings UI where each tab panel is clearly a distinct section of related settings (the Understanding settings example) but the panel titles are <button>/<div> text, not headings, and panels have no role=heading.
Long article that separates topical sections only by large whitespace gaps and a centered decorative <hr>, with bold first lines acting as visual headings but no actual heading elements.
Pricing page of three boxed plan cards ('Starter', 'Pro', 'Enterprise') whose names are styled <strong> at 24pt — visually heading-like, programmatically not headings.

aspects.title: Heading element present but its text does not name/introduce its section (wrong, copy-pasted, placeholder, or generic)
aspects.description: The SC requires headings that 'introduce' their sections and 'clearly indicate the organization of the content' and let users 'know the purpose of each section' — a heading must actually NAME the section it sits above. A page can satisfy the binary presence test while a heading's text is functionally wrong: it describes a DIFFERENT section, was copy-pasted from a template and never updated ('Section Heading', 'Lorem Ipsum'), names the wrong topic (an h2 'Shipping Information' actually heading the returns policy), or is a content-free generic placeholder ('More', 'Stuff', 'Other', 'Untitled') that gives a screen-reader user no orientation. Judging whether a heading's text fits the section body it introduces requires reading both — pure semantic human judgment.
aspects.scLimb: 'they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content' + Benefit 'will know the purpose of each section' — the heading's TEXT must describe its own section (F2-style meaning failure at section level).
aspects.whyUncovered: Every heading in the ACT corpus carries text that genuinely matches its block ('Three Heroes Swear Brotherhood...', 'Content' for nav). No case has a heading whose text is mismatched to, copied across, or generic for its section. Automated tools only verify a heading element exists and is non-empty and exposed; they have no model of a section's meaning and cannot tell that 'Shipping Information' is the wrong name for a returns-policy block, or that 'Section Heading' is a leftover placeholder. Heading-to-content fit is inherently semantic and beyond axe/WAVE/Lighthouse.

references.quote: When such sections exist, they need to have headings that introduce them. This clearly indicates the organization of the content, facilitates navigation within the content, and provides mental "handles" that aid in comprehension of the content.
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
Goal: Users understand how content is organized in sections.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build multi-section pages where every section HAS a real, non-empty, exposed heading element (so axe/047fe0 pass) but the heading TEXT fails to introduce its body. Use four distinct mechanisms across pages: (a) literal CMS placeholder text ('Section Heading' / 'Lorem Ipsum') over finished real content; (b) a heading copied from the section above so it names the previous topic; (c) generic content-free words ('More', 'Stuff', 'Other'); (d) swapped headings (Privacy heading over Notification controls). Bodies must be real, topically specific prose so a reader can see the mismatch. Verdict FAIL.
suggestedScenarios: Page with three sections whose h2 headings are all the literal placeholder 'Section Heading' (left over from a CMS template) over real, distinct bodies.
Article where the h2 over the 'Refund Policy' paragraphs reads 'Shipping & Delivery' (heading copied from the section above and never edited).
Page whose section headings are non-descriptive generic words — h2 'More', h2 'Stuff', h2 'Other' — over substantive, topically-specific bodies.
Multi-section page where headings are correct for sections 1 and 2 but section 3's h2 still reads 'Lorem Ipsum Dolor' though its body is finished real prose.
Settings page where the 'Privacy' h2 sits above the notification controls and the 'Notifications' h2 sits above the privacy toggles (labels swapped).
News page where an h2 'Weather' actually introduces the sports scores and an h2 'Sports' actually introduces the weather forecast.

aspects.title: Multiple distinct navigation/landmark regions, none demarcated by a heading (H69 nav demarcation sub-limb)
aspects.description: H69 calls for heading markup 'to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation.' Real pages frequently carry several distinct navigation regions — a primary top nav, a secondary/left sidebar nav, in-page section nav, and a footer link nav — yet provide a heading for none of them, so a screen-reader user navigating by heading cannot distinguish 'main navigation' from 'footer navigation' from 'related links.' A human must recognize that the page contains several functionally distinct navigation/grouping regions and judge that each needs a section heading to be told apart by AT.
aspects.scLimb: H69 sub-limb: 'demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation' — multiple grouping regions each needing a heading.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus contains only a single <nav> block (its heading text is 'Content'); there is no footer nav, no secondary/left nav, and no page with multiple navigation regions each requiring its own heading. Automated tools detect landmark roles but cannot judge that two functionally distinct navigation regions are genuinely separate sections that each warrant a distinguishing section heading — that is a semantic/structural judgment about the page's organization. (Visually-identical link lists may be different navigation purposes; only meaning distinguishes them.)

references.quote: to demarcate different navigational sections like top or main navigation, left or secondary navigation and footer navigation;
People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.
The objective of this technique is to use section headings to convey the structure of the content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build self-contained pages that contain SEVERAL distinct navigation / grouping regions (primary nav, secondary/left nav, in-page jump nav, footer link nav, social links) rendered as <nav> or <ul> blocks, but provide NO heading for any of them — and provide a single page-level h1 for main content so the document-level check passes. The functional distinctness of the regions must be evident from their link contents (site sections vs legal links vs social vs in-page anchors). Verdict FAIL because the distinct navigation sections lack demarcating headings. Render to confirm the regions read as separate to a sighted user.
suggestedScenarios: Page with a top primary nav (Home/Products/About), a left secondary nav (sub-categories), and a footer nav (Privacy/Terms/Contact) — three navigation regions, no heading on any.
Blog with a main article (h1) plus an unlabeled sidebar of 'related posts' links and an unlabeled footer of social links — two distinct grouping regions with no headings.
Documentation page with an in-page 'On this page' table-of-contents nav and a separate site-section nav, neither carrying a heading.
E-commerce page with category nav, account/utility nav, and footer policy nav stacked as three link lists, none demarcated by a heading.
Dashboard with a global top nav and a workspace-specific left nav, both bare link lists with no section headings to tell them apart by AT.
Portal home with a 'Quick links' group, a 'My tools' group, and a 'Support' group rendered as visually separate link clusters but with no heading on any group.

aspects.title: Heading levels contradict the true content hierarchy (a subsection marked as a sibling, or peers given different levels)
aspects.description: H69 and G141 require headings 'properly nested' so the level structure conveys the logical hierarchy: a subsection should be one level below its parent, and the level numbers should match the topical containment relationships. A page can pass presence and even level-consistency checks while its heading LEVELS misdescribe the actual nesting — e.g. a sub-topic that is logically inside a chapter is marked h2 (sibling of the chapter) instead of h3, or two co-equal major sections are marked h2 and h3 so the second falsely reads as a subsection of the first. Whether a given block is conceptually a subsection of the one above it (and so demands a deeper level) is a content-meaning judgment, NOT the syntactic numeric-skip check that tools perform.
aspects.scLimb: H69/G141 'properly nested' / 'subsections are given subsequent logical levels (h2 is a subsection of h1)' — the LEVEL must reflect the topical containment, applied where the markup is level-consistent but semantically wrong.
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus has exactly one nested case (9b25d8: h1 page title + h2 section) and that nesting is correct; there is NO case where the level assignment contradicts the content's true hierarchy. Crucially, axe-core/Lighthouse flag only empty headings or a RAW NUMERIC skip (e.g. h1 then h4) — they cannot tell whether a block is SEMANTICALLY a subsection of the preceding one, so an h2 that should be h3 (or peers arbitrarily given h2/h3) over level-consistent-looking markup passes automation. Deciding the correct level requires understanding the topical containment between sections. NOTE: scope test pages to the semantic-mismatch case (avoid bare numeric h1->h4 skips, which automation already catches).

references.quote: When headings are nested hierarchically, the most important information is given the highest logical level, and subsections are given subsequent logical levels.(i.e., h2 is a subsection of h1).

To facilitate navigation and understanding of overall document structure, authors should use headings that are properly nested (e.g., h1 followed by h2, h2 followed by h2 or h3, h3 followed by h3 or h4, etc.).

Skipping levels in the sequence of headings may create the impression that the structure of the document has not been properly thought through or that specific headings have been chosen for their visual rendering rather than their meaning.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages with several real, descriptive headings whose level NUMBERS run in a syntactically valid, non-skipping sequence (so axe's numeric heading-order rule passes) but whose levels CONTRADICT the topical containment evident from the prose. Two mechanisms: (a) a sub-topic that elaborates only the section above it is marked as that section's sibling instead of its child; (b) two co-equal peer sections are given different levels so one falsely nests under the other. Real content must make the true parent/child/peer relationship unambiguous to a reader. Verdict FAIL. Deliberately AVOID raw numeric skips (h1->h4) so the case is not auto-detectable.
suggestedScenarios: Chapter page where 'Chapter 1' is h1, three sub-topics are correctly h2, but a sub-sub-point clearly nested inside the second sub-topic is marked h2 (a sibling) instead of h3, flattening the hierarchy — no numeric skip.
Page whose outline reads h1 -> h2 -> h2, yet the second h2 elaborates ONLY the first h2 (it is conceptually its child) so it should be h3; levels say 'sibling', content says 'child'.

Documentation page where two co-equal major sections are marked h2 and h3 respectively (the second arbitrarily demoted), implying the second is a subsection of the first when the content shows they are peers.
FAQ where 'Billing Questions' (h2) is followed by 'Shipping Questions' marked h3 — falsely nesting shipping under billing though they are sibling topic groups.
Guide where a brand-new top-level topic is marked h3 (deeper than the h2 sub-topics above it), so the AT outline implies it belongs under the previous sub-topic when it actually starts a new chapter.
Recipe page where 'Ingredients' and 'Instructions' are both peers but 'Instructions' is marked h3 under the h2 'Ingredients', so the steps read as a subsection of the ingredient list.

aspects.title: Heading element present and exposed but conveying no section name (whitespace-only, decorative-image-only, CSS-image, or dingbat-only)
aspects.description: A heading can satisfy the structural presence requirement — an h2 or role=heading element exists, is visible, and is exposed to AT — yet carry no meaningful accessible name for its section: it holds only whitespace / a non-breaking space, only a decorative , only a CSS background-image of the title text with empty real text, or only ornamental glyphs/dingbats. The screen-reader user hears 'heading, level 2' with no label and gains no orientation; the 'mental handle' the SC promises is absent. Whether the rendered heading actually names the section (versus being functionally empty) is something a human reading the page must judge.
aspects.scLimb: 'headings that introduce them... provides mental "handles"' + Benefit 'will know the purpose of each section' — a present-but-nameless heading provides no section name, a failure mode distinct from a fully-absent heading.
aspects.whyUncovered:
Every ACT heading carries meaningful text. The corpus tests a fully ABSENT heading (4e34ca) and HIDDEN headings (81d501 off-screen, 929079 aria-hidden), but never a heading element that is PRESENT-and-exposed-but-nameless — a distinct failure mode. While a strictly empty

is flagged by axe-core, the human-judgment variants are NOT: an h2 holding only a non-breaking space, only a decorative , only a CSS background-image with empty real text (image-of-text-as-heading without a text alternative — F2/H69 sub-limb), or only dingbat glyphs all look like 'a heading exists' to a tool but provide no section name. Scope test pages to these non-empty-but-meaningless variants, not bare

.

People who are blind will know when they have moved from one section of a web page to another and will know the purpose of each section.

aspects.title: Genuinely unsectioned prose (letter / pre-existing document / continuous narrative) correctly NOT requiring headings
aspects.description: 2.4.10 is Level AAA precisely because 'it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings' — posting a pre-existing document whose author included no headings, or a long letter covering several topics where 'putting headings into a letter would be very strange.' Correctly judging that such a page is NOT in scope (the content is genuinely a single flowing document, not 'organized into sections') versus a page that IS sectioned and merely lacks headings requires reading the prose and deciding whether it has the topical structure the SC targets. This is a content-genre judgment and a false-positive guard: the verdict should be PASS / not-applicable, not a violation.
aspects.scLimb: Applicability gate + AAA inapplicability: 'when posting a pre-existing document... headings that an author did not include in the original document cannot be inserted' and 'a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange.'
aspects.whyUncovered: The corpus models inapplicability with one degenerate artefact (ecc29b: a bare SVG with only a <title>, no HTML document) and one single-paragraph stub (4f112d). Neither models the realistic AAA inapplicability scenario: a multi-paragraph, multi-topic but legitimately heading-less prose document (letter / pre-existing reproduction / continuous narrative) that a human must recognize as out of scope. Automation cannot make this call — it cannot distinguish 'a long letter that legitimately has no headings' from 'a sectioned page missing its headings'; both are just paragraphs with no heading elements. The distinction is entirely about content genre and authorial intent, so this also guards against false-positive flagging.

references.quote: This provision is included at Level AAA because it cannot be applied to all types of content and it may not always be possible to insert headings. For example, when posting a pre-existing document to the web, headings that an author did not include in the original document cannot be inserted.
Or, a long letter would often cover different topics, but putting headings into a letter would be very strange.
What to do: Where content is organized in sections, provide section headings.

A later peer 'Verifying deliveries' is correctly h2. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h2 — no numeric skip.

DELETE and POST are sibling operations on one collection (both should be h2) but DELETE is demoted to h3, asserting a parent/child containment the REST semantics — and the explicit intro sentence — deny; a developer scanning the heading list for the delete endpoint as a top-level operation finds it filed one tier down under POST.

pages.scenario: County government benefits page 'Help with Heating & Cooling Costs' (h1) describing two separate, independently funded programs. LIHEAP is h2 with two correct h3 sub-sections (qualify/apply). The second program, 'Weatherization Assistance Program (WAP)', begins a NEW top-level program but is tagged h3 — the same level as LIHEAP's sub-sections — so WAP and its own sub-sections read as further children of LIHEAP. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h3,h3,h3,h3 — no numeric skip.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': a new top-level section must not be given a subsection level. WAP is a sibling of LIHEAP (should be h2) but sits at h3, so everything from 'Weatherization' onward sounds in the heading outline like more sub-detail of LIHEAP; a user eligible only for WAP, skimming for a second top-level program, never hears a second top-level entry and may conclude the page covers only LIHEAP — an entire benefit is hidden.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The sequence is monotonic with no skipped level, so axe heading-order, Lighthouse and WAVE pass; every heading is non-empty and descriptive. Whether 'Weatherization Assistance Program' continues LIHEAP or starts a new independent program is a meaning judgment that depends on reading the prose ('two separate ... programs ... funded differently'); the numeric pattern and the identical blue heading style give automation nothing to flag.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic community-pharmacy page 'Home Medication Safety Guidelines' (h1, lang=ar dir=rtl) covering two explicitly independent, equal topics: storing medicines (h2) and safe disposal of expired medicines (h3). The intro states the two topics are 'independent and equal' and that 'neither is part of the other', yet disposal is demoted to h3 so it reads as a subsection of storage. A later peer 'When to contact the pharmacist' is correctly h2. Sequence h1,h2,h3,h2 — no numeric skip; lang/dir correct.
pages.mechanism: H69/G141 'properly nested': co-equal topics must share a level. Safe disposal is a peer of storage (should be h2) but is tagged h3, so an Arabic screen-reader user hears storage at level 2 and disposal at level 3 — i.e. that disposal is a sub-part of storage — contradicting the prose that declares the two topics independent and equal. finalReport.title: Section Headings

problems: Caveat (not a defect): SC 2.4.10 is Level AAA, so the 'failed' verdict is an AAA finding. The .md acknowledges this correctly; severity is capped at minor accordingly.

Minor: the EN 301 549 'citation' (third quote in the .md) is informational framing rather than support for the failure mechanism — EN explicitly says clause 9.5 is informative/non-testable. It does not undermine the verdict because the two load-bearing quotes (Understanding 2.4.10 intent + H69 Tests) both verify verbatim and directly support the mechanism.

Minor (non-blocking): the table caption at line 92 uses class="sr-only" but .sr-only is not defined in the <style> block, so the caption is not visually hidden as intended. This is cosmetic and on an unrelated element (the Fees table), not the element under test; it does not affect the 2.4.10 verdict.

Secondary observation (supports, not undermines, the case): the landmark accessible name 'Appeals' (AX region name) diverges from the visible title 'How to appeal a refusal', so even a user switching to the landmarks list gets a terser/different label than sighted users — exactly as the doc claims.

MINOR doc-accuracy nit (not a defect that changes the verdict): the .md/HTML comment claims the ARIA heading and native <h2>s 'share ONE visual style so the page looks uniform' and that the screenshot 'confirms uniform appearance'. The shared CSS rule `h2, .heading-2 { font-size; color; margin; border; padding }` (lines 35-36) omits font-weight, so the native <h2>s render at the UA default bold (700) while the div renders font-weight:400 (normal) — confirmed by inspect computed style fontWeight '400'. The two heading types are therefore NOT pixel-identical in weight. This does not affect AT exposure (programmatic role/level are identical) or the 2.4.10 outcome, but the 'uniform appearance' wording is slightly overstated.

Citation note (not a defect): H69 is an HTML technique whose literal Tests wording ('each section ... starts with a heading') and example use native <h>. The PASS for an ARIA heading rests on G141's broader principle ('Other technologies use other techniques for identifying headers') + the SC text + the ARIA spec, not on H69. The doc uses H69 honestly to characterize the naive-checker failure mode, so this is sound framing, not a misattribution.

Minor (not disqualifying): 2.4.10 is AAA and its Intent text frames sectioning around long documents/chapters/subtopics; a strict reviewer could debate whether four short settings cards are 'sections' in that sense. The case is still defensible because the page is plainly partitioned into four distinct labeled topical groups, which is the situation the SC addresses — but this is exactly the kind of human judgment call the case relies on.

None. This is an intentional PASS boundary variant, not a failing case. The 'errorIsReal' field is false BY DESIGN: the documented outcome is 'passed' and there is correctly no accessibility error. The terminology of the prompt ('confirm the issue is real') is inverted for this PASS card — what must be confirmed is that the page genuinely passes, which it does.

Minor: the .md 'Element / selector carrying the issue' line says 'No issue' but the harness still passes a selector (div[role=heading][aria-level=2]) under the test element; this is consistent and not a defect, just worth noting that the selector identifies a passing heading, not a failing element.

Minor (non-blocking, cosmetic): the table caption uses class 'visually-hidden' but that class is never defined in the page <style> block (lines 19-51), so the caption 'Annual residential permit fees by vehicle count' is actually visually rendered rather than hidden. This does not affect the 2.4.10 heading mechanism at all and does not change the verdict; it is only an authoring nit worth noting.

Potential (theoretical) automated-detectability edge: 'Section Heading' is a recognizable, finite CMS placeholder string. A custom placeholder-dictionary linter could in principle pattern-match it. No shipping checker (axe/WAVE/Lighthouse/validators) does this for heading text, and the deeper 'heading does not describe its section' failure is not lint-catchable, so the case correctly remains human-judgment, but the placeholder text is slightly more pattern-matchable than a purely contextual generic heading.

Minor citation looseness: the .md's third citation (F2) is about a change in text APPEARANCE conveying meaning without semantic markup, which is not the operative mechanism here (heading-vs-body topic mismatch). The .md itself hedges it as 'cited as the WCAG family' rather than a precise rule, and it is not the task's primary 'Claimed citation' (H69), which verifies exactly. Not disqualifying.

Minor scoping nuance: the element-under-test selector is nav.toc, but the documented failure is collective (both nav.docnav and nav.toc lack a demarcating heading). The page is genuinely about the pair; nav.toc is a representative single failing region, which is acceptable but slightly narrows the cited mechanism to one of two regions.

SC 2.4.10 is a Level AAA criterion and both nav regions remain reachable via landmark navigation (the AX tree exposes 2 navigation landmarks), so the real-world harm is an orientation/demarcation gap rather than a blocking failure — hence minor severity, not major.

Interpretive caveat (not a defect): SC 2.4.10's normative core targets CONTENT sections; treating navigation landmarks as 'sections that require a demarcating heading' rests on H69's advisory bullet list. H69 is a sufficient/advisory technique for a Level AAA SC, and the nav regions are already exposed as landmarks. The 'failed' verdict is defensible under the H69 nav-demarcation reading and is exactly the contextual judgment the corpus targets, but a reviewer applying a strict content-only reading of 2.4.10 could call it a borderline/advisory miss rather than a hard failure. This is a legitimate point of debate, not a fabrication.

SC 2.4.10 / H69 nav-demarcation is an inherently debatable sub-limb: the three un-named nav landmarks could alternatively be remediated with aria-label (a 1.3.1/landmark labelling concern) rather than visible section headings, so whether each cluster strictly 'needs' a heading is a judgment call. This does not invalidate the 'failed' label (the cited H69 bullet explicitly authorizes the heading reading), but the case rests on the softer H69 sub-limb rather than a clear-cut 2.4.10 violation. Minor, and arguably the exact kind of judgment the corpus targets.

Element-under-test selector in the prompt is 'aside.rail nav' (region 2 only), but the actual defect spans all three navs (header.top nav, aside.rail nav, footer.foot nav). The .md correctly lists all three; the single-selector framing slightly undersells the page-level mechanism but is not wrong.

No defect — this is the intentional PASS / conformant boundary variant. errorIsReal=false is the correct state for this case (the doc claims expected outcome 'passed', and there is genuinely no accessibility issue).

Minor (non-defect) note: CSS text-transform:uppercase makes the AX accessible names render as 'SECTIONS' / 'RELATED COVERAGE' while the DOM text is 'Sections' / 'Related coverage'. This is purely cosmetic and does not affect conformance; the heading text and landmark names are still meaningful and distinct.

The .vh visually-hidden helper class (line 31) is defined but never applied to any heading — all three nav <h2>s are genuinely visible (target computed style: visibility=visible, opacity=1, box h=12px), so the 'real visible heading' claim holds.

Reliance on AAA interpretation: SC 2.4.10's normative text requires section headings to organize content (which this page satisfies — headings are present and descriptive). The claimed FAIL rests on H69/G141 being read as a requirement that heading LEVEL depth must mirror topical containment depth. That is the standard ACT/techniques interpretation and is defensible, but it is a semantic-judgment call rather than a bright-line normative violation — worth noting that a reviewer could argue the headings 'organize content' adequately and the page technically passes the SC's literal text.

This is still a valid 'failed' under the Understanding doc ('visual presentation is not sufficient to identify document sections'), but it is the subtler edge of 2.4.10 rather than the prototypical missing-heading case.

Outcome label 'failed' sits at a defensible semantic edge: a heading IS structurally present and exposed (role=heading, level=2, non-empty name), so a strict structural reading of 2.4.10 ('are section headings used?') could call it satisfied. The 'failed' verdict relies on the Understanding doc's INTENT (the heading must let a blind user 'know the purpose of each section'), which is correctly cited — but reviewers should note this is a meaning-level call, not a structural one. Not a defect, but a note: the prompt's 'Element under test' selector main p.salutation carries no issue.
